'''''Banksia coccinea''''', commonly known as the '''scarlet banksia''', '''waratah banksia''' or '''Albany banksia''',<ref name= "Wrigley 1991 "/> is an erect shrub or small tree in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Proteaceae]]. Its distribution in the wild is along the [[Southwest Australia|southwest]] coast of [[Western Australia]], from [[Denmark, Western Australia|Denmark]] to the [[Stokes National Park]], and north to the [[Stirling Range]], growing on white or grey sand in [[shrubland]], heath, or open woodland. Reaching up to {{convert|8|m|ft|abbr=on}} in height, it is a single-stemmed plant that has oblong leaves, which are {{convert|3|–|9|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2|–|7|cm|in|1|abbr=on}} wide. The prominent red and white flower [[spike (botany)|spikes]] appear mainly in the spring. As they age, they develop small [[Follicle (fruit)|follicles]] that store seeds until opened by fire. Though widely occurring, it is highly sensitive to [[Phytophthora cinnamomi|dieback]], and large populations of plants have succumbed to the disease.

Collected and described by [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]] in the early 19th century, ''Banksia coccinea'' appears to be most closely related to ''[[Banksia speciosa]]'' and ''[[Banksia baxteri|B. baxteri]]''. ''Banksia coccinea'' plants are killed by [[Bushfires in Australia|bushfire]] and regenerate from seed. The flowers attract nectar- and insect-feeding birds, particularly [[honeyeater]]s, and various insects. Widely considered one of the most attractive ''Banksia'' species, ''B. coccinea'' is a popular garden plant and one of the most important ''Banksia'' species for the [[cut flower]] industry; it is grown commercially in several countries, including Australia, South Africa, Canada, the United States, New Zealand, and Israel. In cultivation, ''B. coccinea'' grows well in a sunny location on well-drained soil, but it cannot survive in areas with humid or wet summers.

The scarlet banksia grows as an erect [[shrub]] or small [[tree]], generally around {{convert|2|–|4|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall, with little lateral spread.<ref name=atlas>{{cite book| last1 = Taylor | first1 = Anne | last2 = Hopper | first2 = Stephen | author-link2 = Stephen Hopper | year=1988 | title = The Banksia Atlas |issue = Australian Flora and Fauna Series Number 8 | pages= 78–79| location = Canberra, Australian Capital Territory | publisher = Australian Government Publishing Service | isbn = 978-0-644-07124-6| title-link = The Banksia Atlas }}</ref> However, it can reach {{convert|8|m|ft|0}} in height, particularly in the vicinity of Albany. The trunk is generally single at the base before branching, covered with smooth grey bark that is {{convert|2|–|5|mm|in|abbr=on|2}} thick and lacking in [[lenticel]]s.<ref name="George 1981">{{cite journal| last = George | first=Alex S. | author-link=Alex George (botanist) | year = 1981 | title = The Genus ''Banksia'' L.f. (Proteaceae) | journal = [[Nuytsia (journal)|Nuytsia]] | volume = 3 | issue = 3 | pages = 239–473 [389–91]| issn = 0085-4417| title-link=The genus Banksia L.f. (Proteaceae) | doi=10.58828/nuy00060 | s2cid=196677407 }}</ref> Peaking in the summer months,<ref name=atlas/> the pinkish-brown new growth is densely hairy. The oblong, cordate or obcordate leaves are {{convert|3|–|9|cm|in|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|2|–|7|cm|in|1|abbr=on}} wide, with {{convert|3|–|5|mm|in|abbr=on}} long [[petiole (botany)|petiole]]s. {{Plantgloss|Truncate}} at the apex, they have [[Dentate leaf|dentate]] margins with small (1–3 mm long) teeth {{convert|3|–|18|mm|in|abbr=on}} apart, separated by shallow u- or v-shaped sinuses. The upper surface is covered in fine fur when young and becomes smooth with age, while the undersurface is covered with white fur, particularly along the midrib.<ref name="George 1981"/>

The flowering process takes 9–12 months; the stems begin developing microscopically in spring, with no visible evidence of flower spike development for around five months before the buds actually appear.<ref name="fuss90">{{cite journal|last1=Fuss|first1=A.M.|last2=Sedgley|first2=M.|date=1990| title=Floral Initiation and Development in Relation to the Time of Flowering in Banksia coccinea R.Br and B. menziesii R.Br (Proteaceae)|journal=Australian Journal of Botany|volume=38|issue=5|pages=487–500|doi=10.1071/BT9900487 |bibcode=1990AuJB...38..487F }}</ref> Flower spikes bloom from May to December or January, peaking between July and October.<ref name=atlas/> The distinctive [[inflorescence]]s arise from the ends of one-year-old branchlets.<ref name="George 1981"/> Squat and roughly cylindrical, they are {{convert|3|–|6|cm|in|abbr=on}} high and {{convert|8|–|10|cm|in|abbr=on|1}} wide.<ref name=Collins>{{cite book| last1 = Collins | first1 = Kevin | last2 = Collins | first2 = Kathy | last3 = George | first3 = Alex S. | pages = 177–78 |title =  Banksias | publisher = Bloomings Books | location = Melbourne, Victoria | year = 2008 | isbn = 978-1-876473-68-6}}</ref> A field study on the southern [[sandplain]]s revealed an average count of around 286 individual flowers on each spike.<ref name="witkowski91">{{cite journal|last1 = Witkowski | first1 = E.T.F. | last2 = Lamont | first2 = Byron B. | author-link2 = Byron Lamont | last3 = Connell | first3 = S.J.|year=1991|title=Seed Bank Dynamics of Three Co-occurring Banksias in South Coastal Western Australia: The Role of Plant Age, Cockatoos, Senescence and Interfire Establishment|journal=Australian Journal of Botany|volume=39|issue=4|pages=385–97|doi=10.1071/BT9910385 | bibcode = 1991AuJB...39..385W }}</ref> The white flower is covered in grey or pale brown fur, with little variation in colour. The [[Gynoecium#pistils|style]] is generally scarlet, but can be dark red, orange, or pink.<ref name="fuss90"/> The [[perianth]] is {{convert|3|–|3.2|cm|in|abbr=on|sigfig=2}} long, while the style is {{convert|4|–|4.8|cm|in|abbr=on|sigfig=2}} long and strongly [[wikt:recurved|recurved]] or looped until they are released at [[anthesis]].<ref name="George 1981"/> Anthesis is acropetal; the flowers open from the base up the spike to the apex.<ref name="fuss90"/> 
The flowers of all banksias arise in a spiral pattern around the flower spike axis; however, in ''Banksia coccinea,'' they develop into distinctive vertical columns, strongly accentuated by large gaps in between.<ref name="George 1981"/> Paired in columns, the red styles contrast with the grey-white perianth, making a striking flower spike.<ref name="Holliday 2008">{{cite book |author1=Holliday, Ivan |author2=Watton, Geoffrey | orig-year = 1975 |year=2008 | title =  Banksias: A Field and Garden Guide | publisher = Australian Plants Society (SA)| location = Adelaide, South Australia | isbn = 978-0-9803013-1-1 | page = 42}}</ref>

The [[infructescence]] is small, with up to 20 small [[Follicle (fruit)|follicles]] concentrated at the lower end of the spike.<ref name=Collins/> Each follicle is {{convert|6|–|8|mm|in|abbr=on|1}} long, {{convert|1|–|2|mm|in|abbr=on|2}} high, and {{cvt|2|–|3|mm|in|2}} wide and usually opens with fire. The {{convert|1.1|–|1.4|cm|in|abbr=on}} long seed is composed of the cuneate (wedge-shaped) seed body proper, measuring  {{convert|0.5|–|0.7|cm|in|abbr=on|sigfig=1}} long and {{convert|0.4|–|0.7|cm|in|abbr=on|sigfig=1}} wide, and a papery [[Glossary of botanical terms#W|wing]]. One side, the outer surface, is grey-black and wrinkled, and the other—the inner surface—protrudes and is black and glistening. The seeds are separated by a dark brown [[seed separator]], roughly the same shape as the seeds, with a depression where the seed body sits adjacent to it in the follicle. It measures {{convert|1.1|–|1.4|cm|in|abbr=on|sigfig=1}} long and {{convert|0.7|–|0.8|cm|in|abbr=on|2}} wide. The dull green [[cotyledon]]s of seedlings are {{convert|0.8|–|0.9|cm|in|abbr=on|sigfig=1}} long and {{convert|0.5|–|0.6|cm|in|abbr=on|2}} wide, described by [[Alex George (botanist)|Alex George]] as "cuneate to [[wikt:obovate|obovate]]". Each cotyledon has a {{convert|1|mm|abbr=on|adj=on|sigfig=1}} [[auricle (botany)|auricle]] at its base. The thick, smooth [[hypocotyl]] is {{convert|1|cm|in|round=0.5|abbr=on}} high and 1.5 mm thick. The seedling leaves are crowded above the cotyledons and linear to spathulate in shape, with recurved and deeply serrated margins with v-shaped sinuses, almost dividing the leaves into triangular lobes. The first pair is {{convert|0.8|–|1.2|cm|in|abbr=on|sigfig=1}} long, with the next 2–4 leaves up to  {{convert|1.7|cm|in|abbr=on|sigfig=1}} long. Successive leaves are more obovate in shape and up to {{convert|4|cm|in|abbr=on|1}} long and {{convert|1.4|cm|in|abbr=on|sigfig=1}} wide. The seedling stems are covered in white hair.<ref name="George 1981"/><!-- cites para -->

===Discovery and naming===
[[File:Banksia coccinea (Illustrationes Florae Novae Hollandiae plate 3).jpg|thumb|right|upright|Plate 3 of [[Ferdinand Bauer]]'s 1813 ''[[Illustrationes Florae Novae Hollandiae]]'']]
The first known specimens of ''Banksia coccinea'' were collected in December 1801, during the visit to [[King George Sound (Western Australia)|King George Sound]] of [[HMS Investigator (1798)|HMS ''Investigator'']] under the command of [[Matthew Flinders]]. [[Botanist]] [[Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773)|Robert Brown]], [[botanical artist]] [[Ferdinand Bauer]], and gardener [[Peter Good]] were on board. All three men gathered plant specimens, but those collected by Bauer and Good were incorporated into Brown's herbarium without attribution, so it is impossible to identify this species's actual collector.<ref name="Hopper 2003">{{cite journal | first = Stephen | last = Hopper | year = 2003 | title= South-western Australia, Cinderella of the world's temperate floristic regions 1 | journal = Curtis's Botanical Magazine | volume = 21 | issue = 2 | pages = 132–79 | doi = 10.1111/1467-8748.00380}}</ref><ref name="Barker 1990">{{cite book | last1 = Barker | first1 = Robyn M. | last2 = Barker | first2 = William R. (Bill) | year = 1990 | chapter = Botanical Contributions Overlooked: the Role and Recognition of Collectors, Horticulturists, Explorers and Others in the Early Documentation of the Australian Flora | editor = Short, Philip S. | title = History of Systematic Botany in Australia | publisher = Australian Systematic Botany Society |location=Canberra, Australian Capital Territory | isbn = 978-0-7316-8463-2 | pages = 37–86}}</ref> The surviving specimen of ''B. coccinea'', held by the [[Natural History Museum, London|Natural History Museum]] in London, is annotated in Brown's hand "King George IIIds Sound Princess Royal Harbour especially near the observatory".<ref name="FloraBase Brown">{{cite web | title = ''Banksia coccinea'' R.Br. | work = Robert Brown's Australian Botanical Specimens, 1801–1805 at the BM | publisher = [[FloraBase]], [[Western Australian Herbarium]] | url = http://florabase.calm.wa.gov.au/brown/search?brname=Banksia+coccinea | archive-url = https://archive.today/20121129185240/http://florabase.calm.wa.gov.au/brown/search?brname=Banksia+coccinea | url-status = dead | archive-date = 29 November 2012 | access-date = 3 January 2010 }}</ref> The observatory was apparently located in what is now the [[central business district]] of [[Albany, Western Australia|Albany]].<ref name="Stehn 2005">{{cite book | last1 = Stehn | first1 = Kay | last2 = George | first2 = Alex | chapter = Chapter 7: Artist in a New Land: William Westall in New Holland | editor1 = Wege, Juliet | editor2 = George, Alex S. | editor3 = Gathe, Jan | editor4 = Lemson, Kris | editor5=Napier, Kath D. | year = 2005 | title = Matthew Flinders and his Scientific Gentlemen | publisher = Western Australian Museum |location=Perth, Western Australia | isbn = 978-1-920843-20-5 | pages = 77–95}}</ref> No further information on the collection is available, as the species is mentioned in neither Brown's nor Good's diary.<ref name="Vallance 2001">{{cite book | first = T. G. | last = Vallance |author2= Moore, D. T.|author3= Groves, E. W. | year = 2001 | title = Nature's Investigator: The Diary of Robert Brown in Australia, 1801–1805 | publisher = Australian Biological Resources Study | location = Canberra, Australian Capital Territory | isbn = 978-0-642-56817-5}}</ref><ref name="Edwards 1981">{{cite journal | editor-last = Edwards | editor-first = Phyllis I. | year = 1981 | title = The Journal of Peter Good: Gardener of Matthew Flinders Voyage to Terra Australis 1801–03 | journal = Bulletin of the British Museum (Natural History), Historical Series | volume = 9 | issue = Complete | pages = 1–213 | doi = 10.5962/p.272300 | issn = 0068-2306| doi-access = free }}</ref>

Good also made a separate seed collection, which included ''B. coccinea'',<ref name="Aiton 1810">{{cite book | first = William | last = Aiton | author-link = William Aiton | year = 1810 | chapter = Banksia | pages = 216 | title = Hortus Kewensis | edition = 2nd | location = London, United Kingdom | publisher = Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown | chapter-url = https://books.google.com/books?id=uRAPAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA216 | access-date = 2010-03-01}}</ref> and Bauer drew the species. Like nearly all of Bauer's field drawings of Proteaceae, the original field sketch of ''B. coccinea'' was destroyed in a [[Hofburg fire]] in 1945.<ref name="Pignatti-Wikus 2000">{{cite journal | first = Erika | last = Pignatti-Wikus | year = 2000 | title = Ferdinand Bauer's Field Drawings of Endemic Western Australian Plants made at King George Sound and Lucky Bay, December 1801 – January 1802. ''I'': Families ''Brassicaceae'', ''Goodenaceae'' p.p., ''Lentibulariaceae'', ''Campanulaceae'' p.p., ''Orchidaceae'', ''Pittosporaceae'' p.p., ''Rutaceae'' p.p., ''Stylidaceae'', ''Xyridaceae'' | journal = Rendiconti Lincei: Scienze Fisiche e Naturali | volume = s.9, v.11 | issue = 2 | pages = 69–109 |author2= Reidl-Dorn, Christa|author3= Mabberley, David | author-link3=David Mabberley}}</ref> However, a [[watercolour]] painting by Bauer, based on his field sketches, still survives at the [[Natural History Museum, London|Natural History Museum]] in [[London]],<ref name="NHM 46923">{{cite web | title = ''Banksia coccinea'', Scarlet Banksia [image details] | publisher = Natural History Museum | url = http://piclib.nhm.ac.uk/piclib/www/image.php?img=46923 | access-date = 1 March 2010 | url-status = dead | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160303175222/http://piclib.nhm.ac.uk/piclib/www/image.php?img=46923 | archive-date = 3 March 2016 }}</ref> and a hand-coloured [[copper engraving]] from that painting was published as Plate 3 of Bauer's 1813 ''[[Illustrationes Florae Novae Hollandiae]]''.<ref name="Bauer 1813">{{cite book | author = Bauer, Ferdinand |author-link=Ferdinand Bauer | year = 1813 | title = Illustrationes Florae Novae Hollandiae | location=London, United Kingdom|publisher=self-published|title-link=:la:wikisource:Illustrationes Florae Novae Hollandiae }}</ref><ref name="Hewson 1999">{{cite book | first = Helen | last = Hewson | year = 1999 | title = Australia: 300 years of Botanical Illustration | publisher = CSIRO Publishing | location = Collingwood, Victoria | isbn = 978-0-643-06366-2}}</ref> German botanist [[Adalbert Schnizlein]] described ''B. purpurea'' in 1843, now regarded as a [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] of ''B. coccinea''.<ref name=apni1>{{APNI | name = ''Banksia purpurea'' Schnizl. | id = 55146}}</ref> Common names include scarlet banksia, waratah banksia, and Albany banksia.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Banksia coccinea''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/rest/instance/apni/51310018 |publisher=APNI|access-date=14 April 2020}}</ref>

Brown published the species in his 1810 ''On the Proteaceae of Jussieu'', its species name derived from the [[Latin]] ''coccineus'' meaning 'scarlet', and referring to the pistils.<ref name = Collins/> He recorded 31 species of ''Banksia'' in his 1810 work ''[[Prodromus Florae Novae Hollandiae et Insulae Van Diemen]]'', and, in his [[Brown's taxonomic arrangement of Banksia|taxonomic arrangement]], placed the taxon in the [[subgenus]] ''[[Banksia verae]]'', the "true banksias", because the inflorescence is a typical ''Banksia'' flower spike.<ref name="Brown 1810">{{cite book | last=Brown | first=Robert | author-link=Robert Brown (botanist, born 1773) | year = 1810 | title = Prodromus Florae Novae Hollandiae et Insulae Van Diemen | publisher = Richard Taylor and Company | location = London, United Kingdom |language= la |page=394 |url = https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/2954550}}</ref> By the time [[Carl Meissner]] published [[Meissner's taxonomic arrangement of Banksia|his 1856 arrangement]] of the genus, there were 58 described ''Banksia'' species. Meissner divided Brown's ''Banksia verae'', which had been renamed ''Eubanksia'' by [[Stephan Endlicher]] in 1847,<ref name="George 1981"/> into four [[Series (botany)|series]] based on leaf properties. He placed ''B. coccinea'' in the series [[Banksia ser. Quercinae|''Quercinae'']].<ref>{{cite book | last = Meissner | first=Carl | author-link = Carl Meissner | year = 1856 | contribution = Proteaceae: ''Quercinae'': ''B. coccinea'' | contribution-url = http://botanicus.org/page/158745 | editor-last = de Candolle | editor-first = A.P. | editor-link = Augustin Pyramus de Candolle | title = Prodromus Systematis Naturalis Regni Vegetabilis, Pars Decima Quarta | location = Paris, France | publisher = Sumptibus Victoris Masson |language = la |volume=14 |page=459 | access-date= 7 Dec 2014 | title-link=Prodromus Systematis Naturalis Regni Vegetabilis }}</ref>

[[George Bentham]] published a thorough revision of ''Banksia'' in his landmark publication ''[[Flora Australiensis]]'' in 1870. In [[Bentham's taxonomic arrangement of Banksia|Bentham's arrangement]], the recognised ''Banksia'' species were reduced from 60 to 46. Bentham defined four [[Section (botany)|sections]] based on leaf, [[style (botany)|style]], and pollen-presenter characters. ''Banksia coccinea'' was placed in section ''Orthostylis''.<ref name="Bentham 1870">{{cite encyclopedia | last = Bentham | first = George | author-link = George Bentham | year = 1870 | title = ''Banksia'' | encyclopedia = [[s:Flora Australiensis|Flora Australiensis]]: Volume 5: Myoporineae to Proteaceae | pages = 541–62 | location = London, United Kingdom| publisher = L. Reeve & Co| title-link = s:Flora Australiensis/Volume V/CIV. Proteaceae/28. Banksia }}</ref>

In 1891, [[Otto Kuntze]], in his ''[[Revisio Generum Plantarum]]'', rejected the generic name ''Banksia'' [[Carolus Linnaeus the Younger|L.f.]], because the name ''Banksia'' had previously been published in 1776 as ''Banksia'' [[Johann Reinhold Forster|J.R.Forst]] & [[Georg Forster|G.Forst]], referring to the genus now known as ''[[Pimelea]]''. Kuntze proposed ''Sirmuellera'' as an alternative, referring to this species as ''Sirmuellera coccinea''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Kuntze |first=Otto |authorlink=Otto Kuntze |title=Revisio generum plantarum |volume=2 |publisher=Arthur Felix |location=Leipzig |year=1891 |pages=581–582 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/4004}}</ref> This application of the [[principle of priority]] was largely ignored by Kuntze's contemporaries,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Rehder |first1=A. |authorlink1=Alfred Rehder |last2=Weatherby |first2=C. A. |authorlink2=Charles Alfred Weatherby |last3=Mansfeld |first3=R. |authorlink3=Rudolf Mansfeld |last4=Green |first4=M. L. |authorlink4=Mary Letitia Green |title=Conservation of Later Generic Homonyms |journal=Bulletin of Miscellaneous Information (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew) |year=1935 |volume=1935 |issue=6/9 |page=368 |doi=10.2307/4107078 |jstor=4107078|doi-access=free }}</ref> and ''Banksia'' L.f. was [[conserved name|formally conserved]], and ''Sirmuellera'' rejected in 1940.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Sprague |first=T. A. |authorlink=Thomas Archibald Sprague |title=Additional Nomina Generica Conservanda (Pteridophyta and Phanerogamae) |journal=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |year=1940 |volume=1940 |issue=3 |doi=10.2307/4111642 |jstor=4111642 |page=99}}</ref>

[[Alex George (botanist)|Alex George]] published a new [[George's taxonomic arrangement of Banksia|taxonomic arrangement]] of ''Banksia'' in his classic 1981 monograph [[The genus Banksia L.f. (Proteaceae)|''The genus ''Banksia'' L.f. (Proteaceae)'']]. Endlicher's ''Eubanksia'' became [[Banksia subg. Banksia|''B.'' subgenus ''Banksia'']], divided into three sections. George placed ''Banksia coccinea'' in its own series—''Banksia'' series ''Coccineae''—within the section [[Banksia sect. Banksia|''B.'' section ''Banksia'']] on account of a unique combination of characters, namely the vertical arrangement of flowers on the spike, combined with the branched open habit, broad leaves, and very small follicles. Members of the series ''Quercinae'' and five species within the series ''[[Banksia ser. Spicigerae|Spicigerae]]'' share the vertically aligned flowers, but do not wholly exhibit the other characters.<ref name="George 1981"/>

[[Kevin Thiele]] and [[Pauline Ladiges]] published a new arrangement for the genus in 1996; their [[morphology (biology)|morphological]] [[Cladistics|cladistic]] analysis yielded a [[cladogram]] significantly different from George's arrangement. They were uncertain of ''B. coccinea'''s placement as it had highly [[autapomorphy|autapomorphic]] characteristics, which made analysis of its relationships difficult. Hence, in [[Thiele and Ladiges' taxonomic arrangement of Banksia|their arrangement]], it was located within the series ''Banksia'' but not allocated to a subseries (''[[incertae sedis]]'').<ref name="Thiele 1996">{{cite journal | last1 = Thiele | first1 = Kevin | author-link1 = Kevin Thiele | last2 = Ladiges | first2 = Pauline Y. | author-link2 = Pauline Ladiges | year = 1996 | title = A Cladistic Analysis of ''Banksia'' (Proteaceae) | journal = [[Australian Systematic Botany]] | volume = 9 | issue = 5 | pages = 661–733 | doi = 10.1071/SB9960661 | bibcode = 1996AuSyB...9..661T }}</ref> It was reclassified in its own section, ''Coccinea,'' in 1996 by Tina Maguire and colleagues; pollen compatibility tests indicated its pollen was most compatible with ''Banksia ericifolia'', ''B. micrantha,'' and ''B. sphaerocarpa'', all of section ''Oncostylis''. However, they did not place it in that section as all members of ''Oncostylis'' have hooked styles at anthesis.<ref name="Maguire 1996">{{cite journal | title=Banksia Sect. ''Coccinea'' (Proteaceae), a New Section |author1=Maguire, Tina L. | author2=Sedgley, Margaret | author3=Conran, J.G. |journal=Australian Systematic Botany |year= 1996 | volume=9|issue=6|pages=887–91 | doi=10.1071/SB9960887 |bibcode=1996AuSyB...9..887M }}</ref> George upheld this in his monograph for the ''[[Flora of Australia (series)|Flora of Australia]]'' series.<ref name="George 1999">{{cite encyclopedia | last = George | first=Alex S. | year = 1999 | title = ''Banksia'' | editor-last = Wilson | editor-first=Annette | encyclopedia = [[Flora of Australia (series)|Flora of Australia]] | volume = 17B: Proteaceae 3: ''Hakea'' to ''Dryandra'' | pages = 175–251 [175–76, 227] | publisher = CSIRO Publishing / [[Australian Biological Resources Study]] |location=Collingwood, Victoria |isbn = 978-0-643-06454-6}}</ref> ''B. coccinea''<nowiki>'</nowiki>s placement within ''Banksia,'' according to the ''Flora of Australia,'' is as follows:

:'''Genus ''[[Banksia]]'''''
::'''Subgenus ''[[Banksia subg. Banksia|Banksia]]'''''
:::'''Section ''Banksia sect. Coccineae'''''
:::::''B. coccinea''

In 2002, a [[molecular phylogenetics|molecular]] study by [[Austin Mast]] again showed ''Banksia coccinea'' to be the next closest relative of a group comprising ''Banksia speciosa'' and ''B. baxteri'' and only distantly related to other members of the series ''Banksia''.<ref name="Mast 2002">{{cite journal | first1 = Austin R. | last1 = Mast | author-link1 = Austin Mast | last2 = Givnish | first2 = Thomas J. | author-link2 = Thomas J. Givnish | year = 2002 | title = Historical Biogeography and the Origin of Stomatal Distributions in ''Banksia'' and ''Dryandra'' (Proteaceae) Based on their cpDNA Phylogeny | journal = American Journal of Botany | volume = 89 | issue = 8 | pages = 1311–23 | doi = 10.3732/ajb.89.8.1311 | issn = 0002-9122 | pmid = 21665734 | doi-access = free }}</ref> This was reinforced in a 2013 molecular study by Marcel Cardillo and colleagues using chloroplast DNA and combining it with earlier results.<ref name="cardillo 2013">{{cite journal|last=Cardillo|first=Marcel|author2=Pratt, Renae|date=2013|title=Evolution of a Hotspot Genus: Geographic Variation in Speciation and Extinction Rates in ''Banksia'' (Proteaceae)|journal=BMC Evolutionary Biology|volume=13|issue=155|pages=155| doi=10.1186/1471-2148-13-155|pmid=23957450|pmc=3751403 |bibcode=2013BMCEE..13..155C |doi-access=free }}</ref>

Mast, Eric Jones, and Shawn Havery published the results of their cladistic analyses of [[DNA sequence]] data for ''Banksia'' in 2005. They inferred a [[phylogeny]] greatly different from the accepted taxonomic arrangement, including finding ''Banksia'' to be [[paraphyly|paraphyletic]] with respect to ''[[Banksia ser. Dryandra|Dryandra]]''.<ref name="Mast 2005">{{cite journal | last1 = Mast | first1 = Austin R. | last2 = Jones | first2 = Eric H. | last3 = Havery | first3 = Shawn P. | year = 2005 | volume = 18 | issue = 1 | title = An Assessment of Old and New DNA Sequence Evidence for the Paraphyly of ''Banksia'' with Respect to ''Dryandra'' (Proteaceae) | journal = [[Australian Systematic Botany]] | pages = 75–88 | doi = 10.1071/SB04015 | bibcode = 2005AuSyB..18...75M }}</ref> A new taxonomic arrangement was not published at the time, but early in 2007, Mast and Thiele initiated a rearrangement by transferring ''Dryandra'' to ''Banksia'', and publishing [[Banksia subg. Spathulatae|''B.'' subgenus ''Spathulatae'']] for the species having spoon-shaped cotyledons; in this way, they also redefined the [[autonym (botany)|autonym]] ''B.'' subg. ''Banksia''. They foreshadowed publishing a full arrangement once DNA [[sampling (statistics)|sampling]] of ''Dryandra'' was complete. In the meantime, if Mast and Thiele's nomenclatural changes are taken as an interim arrangement, then ''B. coccinea'' is placed in ''B.'' subg. ''Banksia''.<ref name="Mast 2007">{{cite journal | last1 = Mast | first1 = Austin R. | last2 = Thiele | first2 = Kevin | year = 2007 | title = The Transfer of ''Dryandra'' R.Br. to ''Banksia'' L.f. (Proteaceae) | journal = [[Australian Systematic Botany]] | volume = 20 | issue = 1 | pages = 63–71 | doi = 10.1071/SB06016 | bibcode = 2007AuSyB..20...63M }}</ref>

No subspecies are recognised, although DNA analysis showed that a population at Redmond was genetically distinctive, while those at [[Gull Rock National Park|Gull Rock]], [[Two Peoples Bay Nature Reserve|Two Peoples Bay]], and Cheyne Beach were unusually diverse.<ref name="Rieger 1998">{{cite journal|author1=Rieger, M. |author2=Sedgley, M.A |date=1998|title=Preliminary Investigation of Genetic Variation within and between Cultivated and Natural Populations of ''Banksia coccinea'' and ''Banksia menziesii''|journal=Australian Journal of Botany|volume=46|issue=4|pages=547–58|doi=10.1071/BT96102 |bibcode=1998AuJB...46..547R }}</ref>

[[Noongar]] people know the tree as '''Waddib'''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.kippleonline.net/bobhoward/plantsframe.html|title=Noongar names for plants|access-date=24 November 2016|publisher=kippleonline.net|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161120071826/http://www.kippleonline.net/bobhoward/plantsframe.html|archive-date=20 November 2016}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Banksiacoccineargemap.png|thumb|right|upright|Range along the southern West Australian coast]]
''Banksia coccinea'' occurs close to the south coast of Western Australia, from the Hay River northeast of [[Denmark, Western Australia|Denmark]], [[Albany, Western Australia|Albany]] in the west, east to [[Stokes National Park]] southeast of [[Munglinup]], and inland to the [[Stirling Range]] and the northern border of [[Fitzgerald River National Park]]. Around 47% of plants are protected in conservation areas, while 13% are on road verges.<ref name="atlas" /><!-- cites two previous sentences --> It prefers deep white or grey sand, among tall shrubland, heath, mallee-heath, associated with such species as ''[[Banksia baxteri|B. baxteri]]'', ''[[Banksia speciosa|B. speciosa]]'', ''[[Banksia attenuata|B. attenuata]],'' and ''[[Lambertia inermis]]'', or low open woodland in the Stirling Range and near Albany, where it is found with ''[[Eucalyptus marginata]]'', ''Banksia attenuata,'' and ''[[Banksia ilicifolia|B. ilicifolia]]''.<ref name="George 1981"/> Most of its range has a gently undulating topography, but it also occurs on a steep rocky slope at Ellen Peak in the Stirling Ranges.<ref name=atlas/> The annual rainfall is {{convert|400|–|800|mm|in|abbr=on|sigfig=2}}.<ref name="George 1996">{{cite book| last1 = George | first1 = Alex S. | year = 1996 | title = The Banksia Book | edition = 3rd | location = Kenthurst, New South Wales | page = 176 | publisher = Kangaroo Press (in association with the Society for Growing Australian Plants) | isbn = 978-0-86417-818-3}}</ref>

==Ecology==
[[File:Banksia coccinea.jpg|thumb|''Banksia coccinea'' at [[Gull Rock National Park]]]]
A field study conducted around [[Albany, Western Australia|Albany]] found the [[honey possum]] (''Tarsipes rostratus'') sometimes visits ''Banksia coccinea'', as do the [[New Holland honeyeater]] (''Phylidonyris novaehollandiae''), [[white-cheeked honeyeater]] (''P. nigra''),<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Weins, Delbert|author2=Renfree, Marilyn|author3=Wooller, Ronald D.|year=1979|title=Pollen loads of Honey possums (''Tarsipes spencerae'') and non-flying mammal pollination in South-western Australia|journal=Annals of the Missouri Botanical Garden|volume=66|pages=830–38|url=http://www.botanicus.org/item/31753003566442|access-date=24 November 2010|doi=10.2307/2398921|issue=4|jstor=2398921 |bibcode=1979AnMBG..66..830W }}</ref> and [[western spinebill]] (''Acanthorhynchus superciliosus'').<ref name=atlas/> ''Banksia coccinea'' flowers are visited by [[colletidae|colletid]] bees ''[[Hylaeus alcyoneus]]'' and  ''[[Hylaeus sanguinipictus|H. sanguinipictus]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://flyaqis.museum.vic.gov.au/cgi-bin/texhtml |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060824174104/http://flyaqis.museum.vic.gov.au/cgi-bin/texhtml |url-status=dead |archive-date=24 August 2006 |title=Specimen Report |year=2010 |work=Museum Victoria website: Bioinformatics |publisher=Museum Victoria |access-date=25 November 2010 |location=Melbourne, Victoria }}</ref> The [[short-billed black cockatoo]] breaks off old cones with follicles to eat the seed, often doing so before the seed is ripe.<ref name="witkowski91"/>

''B. coccinea'' is killed by fire and regenerates from seed released from burnt follicles.<ref name="George 1981"/> It has some degree of [[serotiny]], that is, it has an [[Canopy seed bank|aerial seed bank]] in its [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]] in the form of the follicles of the old flower spikes. However, seed numbers are less than other co-occurring banksia species on the southern plains and peak several years after a fire. Unusually for banksias, ''B. coccinea'' can release seed with resulting seedlings growing in the absence of a bushfire trigger. Plants flower and fruit three years after germination and are shorter-lived than other banksias, appearing in poor health or dying before 20 years of age. They appear to be suited to fire intervals of less than 20 years.<ref name="witkowski91"/>

Manipulating growing conditions on plants in cultivation showed that longer daylight (16 hours vs 8 hours) led to the development of more flower spikes, indicating that flower initiation was related to day length.<ref name="Rieger 1996">{{cite journal|author1=Rieger, M. |author2=Sedgley, M.A |date=1996|title=Effect of daylength and temperature on flowering of the cut flower species Banksia coccinea and Banksia hookeriana|journal=Australian Journal of Experimental Agriculture|volume=36|issue=6|pages=747–53|doi=10.1071/EA9960747}}</ref>

Extremely sensitive to dieback caused by ''[[Phytophthora cinnamomi]]'',<ref name="McCredia 1985">{{cite journal | first = Thomas A. | last = McCredie | year = 1985 | title = Variability in the resistance of ''Banksia'' L.f. species to ''Phytophthora cinnamomi'' Rands | journal = [[Australian Journal of Botany]] | volume = 33 | issue = 6 | pages = 629–37 | doi = 10.1071/BT9850629 |author2=  Dixon, Kingsley W.|author3= Sivasithamparam, K. | bibcode = 1985AuJB...33..629M }}</ref> ''Banksia coccinea'' is an [[indicator species]] for the presence of the disease.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dec.wa.gov.au/pdf/projects/dieback/dieback_indicators.pdf |title=Common Indicator Species for the Presence of Disease caused by ''Phytophthora cinnamomi'' |publisher=Government of Western Australia |access-date=10 April 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110319210839/http://www.dec.wa.gov.au/pdf/projects/dieback/dieback_indicators.pdf |archive-date=19 March 2011 }}</ref> There is no known means of eradicating dieback. Much of the Stirling Range National Park is infested, though Fitzgerald River National Park has been largely spared.<ref name="Barrett 2005">{{cite journal|last=Barrett|first=Sarah|date=2005|title=Conservation of Flora and Plant Communities Threatened by 'Phytophthora dieback' in Southern Western Australia|journal=Australasian Plant Conservation: Journal of the Australian Network for Plant Conservation|volume=13|issue=4|pages=16–17|issn=1039-6500}}</ref> Applying [[phosphite]] to infested areas has been shown to reduce the mortality rates to around 50%.<ref name="shearer 2007">{{cite journal|author1=Shearer, Bryan L. |author2=Fairman, Richard G. |date=2007|title=Application of phosphite in a high-volume foliar spray delays and reduces the rate of mortality of four Banksia species infected with Phytophthora cinnamomi|journal=Australasian Plant Pathology|volume=36|issue=4|pages=358–68|doi=10.1071/AP07033|bibcode=2007AuPP...36..358S |s2cid=2746387 }}</ref> ''B. coccinea'' has shown some symptoms of toxicity to the application of phosphite, with some patchy necrosis of leaves, but the plant's uptake of the compound is somewhat lower compared with other shrub species. Unusually, the symptoms do not appear to be proportional to exposure levels.<ref>{{cite journal| title= Phytotoxicity in relation to ''in planta'' concentration of the fungicide phosphite in nine Western Australian native species|author1=Barrett, Sarah R.|author2=Shearer, Bryan L|author3=Hardy G.E.S |journal=Australasian Plant Pathology|volume=33|issue=4|pages=521–28| doi= 10.1071/AP04055| year= 2004|bibcode=2004AuPP...33..521B |s2cid=35522990}}</ref>

Dying stands of ''B. coccinea'' were observed in 1989, and the fungus ''[[Cryptodiaporthe melanocraspedia]]'' was isolated as the cause in 1995. The disease, a form of aerial [[canker]], manifested initially as dead, dry, brown leaves and the tips of new growth. Plants would die from the top downwards, with larger branches affected over time. Under the outer bark, orange and brown patches of necrosis spread out from leaf nodes until they encircle the stem, which then dies. Flower spikes may be affected during the flowering season. In humid spells during warm weather, white or pink spore tendrils are produced on dead wood. One affected stand monitored over three years from October 1989 to June 1992 showed a 97% mortality of plants (compared with a baseline 40%). Investigators Bryan Shearer and colleagues isolated another virulent pathogen that they identified as a species of ''[[Zythiostroma]]''; however, it appeared to invoke an immune response in the plant. This immune response, coupled with the fact that it had not been observed in the wild, led them to believe it was not a major pathogen of the species.<ref name="Shearer 1995">{{cite journal|last=Shearer|first=Bryan L. |author2=Fairman, Richard G. |author3=Bathgate, J.A. |date=1995|title=''Cryptodiaporthe melanocraspeda'' Canker as a Threat to ''Banksia coccinea'' on the South Coast of Western Australia.|journal=Plant Disease|volume=79|issue=6 |pages=637–41|url=http://www.apsnet.org/publications/PlantDisease/BackIssues/Documents/1995Articles/PlantDisease79n06_637.pdf |doi=10.1094/PD-79-0637 |bibcode=1995PlDis..79..637S }}</ref> This species has since been reclassified and named as ''[[Luteocirrhus shearii]]''.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Crane, Colin |author2=Burgess, Treena I. |date=2013|title=''Luteocirrhus shearii'' gen. sp. nov. (Diaporthales, Cryphonectriaceae) pathogenic to Proteaceae in the South Western Australian Floristic Region|journal=IMA Fungus|volume=4|issue=1|pages=111–22|doi = 10.5598/imafungus.2013.04.01.11|pmid=23898417|pmc=3719199}}</ref>

''B. coccinea'' is a host for the gall midge ''[[Dasineura banksiae]]'', a species of [[diptera|fly]] that attacks and lays eggs on the leaves between late October and early December. The round white hairy galls are 5–7 mm in diameter and generally contain one larva, or up to five on severely infested plants. The larvae moult and feed from January to March, when they reduce activity until early October. Although these are not harmful to the plant, they disfigure the cut foliage, reducing its value.<ref name="kolesik">{{cite journal|author1=Kolesik, Peter |author2=Woods, Bill |author3=Crowhurst, Max |author4=Wirthensohn, Michelle G |date=2007|title=Dasineura banksiae: a new species of gall midge (Diptera: Cecidomyiidae) feeding on Banksia coccinea (Proteaceae) in Australia|journal=Australian Journal of Entomology|volume=46|issue=1|pages=40–44|doi=10.1111/j.1440-6055.2007.00584.x}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
Widely considered one of the most attractive ''Banksia'' species, ''B. coccinea'' is a popular garden plant and one of the most important ''Banksia'' species for the cut flower industry; it is grown commercially in Australia, South Africa, Canada, the United States, New Zealand, Israel, and trialled in France, Spain, and South America.<ref name=Collins/> Its striking terminal inflorescences and furry new growth are its main horticultural attributes. However, it is highly sensitive to dieback and succumbs readily when exposed. It is difficult to keep alive in areas of heavy soils, summer rainfall, or humidity, such as the Australian east coast. Furthermore, flowering may be sparse or not occur when cultivated in warmer climates such as Perth.<ref name=Collins/> Pruning promotes branching, which leads to more flower spikes being produced.<ref name = "Wrigley 1991"/>

Propagation is by seed, though these can be difficult to extract from the follicles.<ref name = "Wrigley 1991">{{cite book | last1 = Wrigley | first1 = John | last2 = Fagg | first2=Murray | title = Banksias, Waratahs and Grevilleas | year = 1991 | publisher = Angus & Robertson | location = Sydney, New South Wales | isbn = 978-0-207-17277-9|pages = 92–93}}</ref> Seeds do not require any treatment before sowing, and [[germinate|germination]] takes 12 to 48 days.<ref name="Sweedman 2006">{{cite book | editor-last1 = Sweedman | editor-first1 = Luke | editor-last2= Merritt | editor-first2=David | year = 2006 | title = Australian seeds: a guide to their collection, identification and biology | publisher = CSIRO Publishing | isbn = 978-0-643-09298-3 | page = 203}}</ref> Cultivars require propagation by cutting for progeny to grow true. Cuttings are slow to strike.<ref name=Collins/> Attempts to graft ''B. coccinea'' have met with little success.<ref name = "Wrigley 1991"/>

In a breeding program conducted by [[Margaret Sedgley]] of the Department of Horticulture, Viticulture and Oenology, [[University of Adelaide#Waite|Waite Agricultural Research Institute]]  of the [[University of Adelaide]] in [[Adelaide]], [[South Australia]], two forms of ''Banksia coccinea'' were bred, registered under [[plant breeders' rights]] (PBR), and commercially propagated, mainly for the cut flower industry. ''Banksia'' [[Banksia 'Waite Flame'|'Waite Flame']] is an early flowering, somewhat orange-hued form, and ''B.'' [[Banksia 'Waite Crimson'|'Waite Crimson']] is a red-flowering form that peaks mid-season.<ref name="Holliday 2008"/><!-- cites previous two sentences -->
